content:
molly: Heads-up — saw a perf regression on the runtime with a KV-cache heavy workload after yesterday's rollout. p50 up ~20% and token throughput down. I tried an nsys trace inside the k8s pod but the .qdrep is missing CUDA kernels (host-level trace shows kernels normally). Could be container permissions or toolkit issues.

sam: Which profiler/command did you run? nsys, nvprof, perfetto?

molly: nsys. Command: ```nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --output=/tmp/run1 --target-pid=$(pidof runtime_server)``` Ran that inside the app pod. The collector ran but the resulting report shows only user threads and no GPU kernels. On the host, running the same trace captures kernels as expected.

jason: Historically, nsys inside a non-privileged container can miss kernel timelines because it can't access some proc entries or device nodes. Are /dev/nvidia* and /dev/nvhost present in the pod? Are we using the nvidia-container-toolkit and the device plugin mounts?

molly: The pod spec uses the GPU device plugin (we get gpus allocated) but the cluster is configured rootless (kubelet without privileged). We don't set privileged: true. Inside the pod: `ls -l /dev/nvidia*` returns "no such file or directory" but nvidia-smi works via driver? Strange output. I suspect the toolkit isn't creating the per-container /run/nvidia mounts due to missing mount permissions.

ana: Do you have the stderr from nsys? I remember seeing "Failed to open /proc/<pid>/task/<tid>/syscall: Permission denied" in similar cases.

molly: Paste of nsys stderr: ```nsys: WARNING: Failed to collect kernel timeline: /proc/1234/task/5678/syscall: Permission denied
nsys: INFO: Recording completed, report contains host only events
```

perfbot: Automated: Added label perf-investigation, created perf ticket PERF-4521.

sam: Quick repro steps to validate permission hypothesis: 1) spin up a debug pod with securityContext.privileged: true and same image; 2) mount host /dev and /run/nvidia to the pod; 3) run nsys inside privileged pod and compare qdrep. If privileged capture shows kernels and non-priv doesn't, it's permissions. Also try pid: host (share PID namespace) as a second check.

jason: Also check nvidia-container-toolkit version — older toolkit won't populate /run/nvidia or relay the device environment properly in rootless setups. And verify the driver versions on nodes (we had a node upgrade last week). Some driver changes break kernel symbol resolution for nsys.

ana: If you can get a privileged capture, please look for hot kernels. In a quick host trace I ran yesterday (same workload) the majority of GPU time is in two kernels: `gemm_int8` and `softmax_fwd` (names differ by build) — combined ~70% of GPU time. If those disappear from container trace, the runtime falls back to a slower codepath that does more host-side memcpy and CPU spin.

molly: Did a quick smoke: launched a privileged debug pod, mounted /dev/nvidia0 and /run/nvidia, ran nsys and we captured kernels. Hotspots: ```
GPU kernels:
 - gemm_int8_kernel_v3  48% GPU time
 - softmax_fwd_kernel   22% GPU time
CPU hotspots:
 - kv_cache::fallback_copy  (more frequent under non-privileged)
```

molly: Under non-priv pod the runtime chooses a different kernel selection path (fallback quantized->reference) which triggers extra CPU memcpy and higher p50. Likely the runtime detected missing kernel support and switched to a compatibility implementation.

jason: That aligns with a recent change in the kernel selection logic where we probe for kernel availability via nvml/nvtools and fallback to reference if probe fails. If the probe fails inside container due to missing device nodes or insufficient permissions, runtime will pick the safer (slower) path. We should make probing more robust and add a caching override for clusters that are rootless.

ana: Action items: molly attach the privileged and non-priv qdreps and the pod yaml -> link: gs://redwood-perf/molly/1782001234/ (molly uploaded run1.qdrep and run1-nopriv.qdrep). jason to inventory node driver versions across the cluster and confirm toolkit version. sam to try a small patch to the runtime to skip probe when env REDWOOD_FORCE_KERNEL_PROBE=1 (or rather a flag to force assume kernels exist for testing). I'll run a host-level perfetto to cross-validate timestamps.

molly: Quick note — the node that routed work to the slow path had driver 535.102; others had 548.x. Filing a node rollout rollback for the suspect nodes. :rotating_light:

sam: Also consider adding a diagnostic in the runtime that logs kernel probe outcome at startup (one-time) and emits a metric so we can alert if a node/cluster is probing failed kernels. That would make these regressions obvious earlier.

jason: Agreed. I'll open a small RFC for the probe telemetry + an env override for testing.

molly: Thanks all. I'll leave the privileged debug pod running for anyone who wants to attach and will drop the qdrep links in PERF-4521. :thumbsup:
